# Canary

Updated: 2026-10-29 12:41 CET

Version 3.30 buys back a held index hedge through `canary proposals reduce`,
and the hedge plan offers only a sale Canary can place when asked. A hedge
table deleted from the risk policy stays deleted. The daemon removes its own
old policy backups after a successful start.

Version 3.29 adds reduction-plan comparisons for index falls and rises, loss
room and quoted trading costs, plus index-hedge planning. Optional IV-fallback
policy reports uncertainty when a held option lacks its own volatility.
Plans are not submission authority.

Version 3.28 adds historical option-exit replay, option-list pagination and
intraday account-value history. Holding locks cover a name across its held
contracts. Mandate reporting separates the loss measure from volatility;
proposal reviews include an index-fall comparison when it can be measured.
Historical replays are not forecasts or instructions to trade.

Version 3.27 adds stock-entry reviews with optional protection for the added
shares, call discovery and budget-based call sizing, and holding locks for
bulk and automatic reductions. CLI help includes JSON request examples.
Reduction checks account for Canary's working combo legs and wait when known
fills and positions disagree. Existing written limits are preserved; policy
migration adds missing reduction-allowance fields (1% for stocks/ETFs and 5%
for options). Standard binaries and MCP remain read-only, and MCP cannot
preview or submit orders.

Version 3.26 says in plain words which TWS or IB Gateway settings differ
from what Canary needs: `canary status` gains a Gateway setup row, read once
after each connect, and Canary never changes a setting. When the Gateway
answers the open-order request late, as during IBKR's nightly reset, the
daemon now redials its connection instead of reading no open orders until a
restart. Existing policies load unchanged; standard binaries and MCP remain
read-only.

Version 3.25 lets every live strategy in the register trade, not only the
core: each entry written live turns its month's decision into a row of its
own on its own line, with the core's terms, gates and standing-mandate path,
and its fills count in its own sleeve. A strategy whose traded share class
is young can read its trend on an older class of the same fund until its
own closes fill the window. The second strategy, a managed-futures fund on
its EUR-hedged Xetra line, can be written into the register. Existing
policies load unchanged; standard binaries and MCP remain read-only.

Version 3.24 lets the desk's arming reach the strategies: Canary serves a
submit path for the standing automatic mandate the owner confirms once on
their device, so a controller can send a served strategy row, the core
sleeve's monthly buy included, through the one order path with every gate
re-checked; nothing is sent until the controller presents that mandate. The
decision scorecard can now conclude: one unit of evidence per name and week,
overlap charged, the market taken out on SPY and the sector fund, a placebo
and a futility test, and each decision's fill cost. The owner's sleeve gets a
drawdown stop of its own. Existing policies load unchanged; standard binaries
and MCP remain read-only.

Version 3.23 adds one strategy evaluator that runs every machine strategy in
the risk policy's register: the core sleeve's rule is its first entry,
unchanged, and a second strategy is a table naming its fund, a signal from the
library and the owner's numbers (`canary strategy ID` shows what it would
trade). The core sleeve can go live at a small stage: with its stage written,
each monthly decision becomes one proposal row the owner confirms on their
device, and the daemon never sends it by itself. Every entry runs in shadow
until the owner writes its stage. Existing policies load unchanged; standard
binaries and MCP remain read-only.

Version 3.22 adds the owner's mandate: a whole-book risk budget measured by
historical simulation, refusals of risk-adding orders while the book is over
it, a pre-authorised forced reduction with a veto window, and risk
allocations per sleeve. A decision scorecard scores every position change per
sleeve with sequential evidence, and a quote kept at every fill measures the
spread paid. A strategy register in the risk policy names each machine
strategy; the core sleeve runs read-only in shadow; an option-chain recorder
saves the desk's chains once a session. Hand orders in TWS can be cancelled or
changed from Canary when the owner enables it, and two Canary orders never
sell the same shares twice. Cash interest rates come from the broker's
statement. Existing policies load unchanged; standard binaries and MCP remain
read-only.

Version 3.21 adds owner-confirmed order queues and whole-position stock trailing
protection in trading builds. It fixes large volume readings and keeps explicitly
deactivated orders visible without counting them as active protection. A read-only
CLI diagnostic reports supported TWS and Gateway API settings as part of
TWS / IB Gateway 10.50 compatibility hardening. The main connection keeps its
tested protocol. Live validation used TWS; Gateway 10.50 still needs an end-to-end
check. Existing policies and broker settings stay
unchanged. Standard binaries and MCP remain read-only.

Version 3.20 adds exact or maximum stock sizing and read-only portfolio planning
against explicit, expiring owner targets. Routine monitoring reuses verified
statement and order-history work to reduce CPU use. The drawdown brake refuses
risk-adding orders while engaged or when required evidence is unavailable.
Desk mandate records and request lookup do not expose execution submission or
activate automatic trading. Standard binaries and MCP remain read-only.

Version 3.19 adds owner-approved currency repayments, gated bill and bond orders
by ISIN or CUSIP, and bond yield, duration and rate-risk measurements. Currency
leveling starts disabled and cannot be pre-authorised. Bond-risk measurements
introduce no new warnings or blocks. Cash settings and risk presets are served
from the daemon; order-limit changes require verified device confirmation.
Qualifying exits can pass the notional and option-contract caps only when they
reduce absolute net delta for both their underlying and the portfolio, fit
beside working orders and satisfy the option-cover checks. This also applies
to existing pre-authorised exit buckets, with their notice and veto window.
Existing written policy limits are preserved; newly written defaults are 10%
of net liquidation value and 10 option contracts. Standard binaries and MCP
remain read-only.

Version 3.18 introduced the following features. It shows every limit in force and checks that the limits add up.
`canary policy show --explain` prints every limit, policy and runtime setting
that governs Canary, each with its value, unit, source and meaning, and `canary
policy show SECTION` prints one part. `canary policy check` reads the config and
the policy files against each other and, through the daemon, against the live
account (`--offline` checks the files alone), and names each implausible value
with a reason and, where one applies, a suggested fix. MCP clients get the same
report from the read-only `canary_policy_check` tool, which never changes a
limit. The per-order limits now live in the risk constitution,
`risk-policy.toml` `[order_limits]`, and the order-value cap scales with net
liquidation value between a floor and ceiling in the policy file. A temporary
larger cap is one override that Canary records in its journal. The cash sweep's
reserve follows net liquidation value and planned needs, each bill order stays
between a minimum and a maximum size and bill buys wait while any currency is
borrowed. The daemon now produces the portfolio stress verdict and the position
risk flags; the CLI, MCP tools, app and Go client show the installed daemon's
answer. `canary setups coverage`, `options` and `markouts` print readable output
by default (`--json` returns the previous output), and the status, market,
macro, proposal and data-health views lead with what needs attention. In trading
builds the order-value cap and the short-sale check no longer refuse a
broker-side stop that, with the other working sell orders for the same stock or
ETF, sells no more than the long position, and a protective stop guard writes on
its own, but only to shrink or cancel stop orders Canary itself placed when the
position falls below them. Stops placed by hand are never changed. Version 3.18.1
introduced automatic policy migration: at its first start the daemon backs up
each file it changes and writes the missing keys. That release wrote a 5% of
net liquidation scale with a 100,000 base-currency ceiling. Version 3.19 writes
10% and 10 option contracts only for new or missing keys; existing written
values are preserved and the 100,000 ceiling is unchanged. The sweep remains off by default. Owner commissioning requires
calibrated reserves and current native settlement evidence; missing evidence
holds the sweep. Bills can lose value on an early sale. Standard binaries and
the MCP server remain read-only. Installation does not enable automatic
submission or grant broker-write permission.

Canary is a local risk desk for a brokerage account: a daemon, shell CLI,
read-only MCP server, paired app, and a public Go module with a daemon client
and the TWS wire protocol. It works with Interactive Brokers today (IB Gateway
or TWS); the broker layer is a separate Go package,
`github.com/osauer/canary/v2/pkg/ibkr`, so other platforms can follow. The
daemon owns account scope, market sensors, rulebook evaluation, protection
proposals, option-exercise opportunities, and typed source quality. The CLI, MCP
server, and app are adapters over that authority.

Canary is an independent personal project by Oliver Sauer.

Canary v3.17.0 adds a durable owner watchlist, read-only volume-turn
observations, standard-call discovery, setup coverage and entry markouts through
the CLI and typed Go reads. Setup parameters are unvalidated observations, and
historical reconstruction does not establish what was known at the original
decision. Markouts use later quotes for qualifying Canary-placed fills, exclude
commissions and never replace account P/L; missed targets stay missing. These
setup tools have no MCP surface. Watchlist edits change local preferences only.
CLI and read-only MCP add indicative borrowing-rate discovery, dated price and
liquidity context, and FINRA short-interest screens. Borrower costs are not
lender yields. FINRA positions are twice-monthly reports; percentage of free
float remains unavailable. Source dates and partial market coverage stay visible.

Canary v3.16.0 adds lending observations to the signed binaries and MCPB.
The read-only `canary lending fees --json` command and `canary_lending_fees`
MCP tool expose bounded customer net-fee history from retained IBKR statements. The app shows
dated position loan annotations and expandable fees; Desk's analyst can read
the same evidence. Missing sections, partial coverage and complete zero are
distinct. Participation stays with IBKR. Fees are not added to account P&L:
payment status and P&L/accrual linkage remain unproved. Populated account reports
are still needed for commissioning. Borrow Fee Details describes short-borrow
costs; it is not earned lending income. Forex P&L Details describes currency
transactions and realised lots; it is not the valuation contribution reported
by `canary reporting fx`.
See https://osauer.dev/canary/docs/understand/edge.html#stock-lending-income.

Canary v3.16.0 adds FX contribution to the signed binaries and MCPB.
`canary reporting fx`, `canary_reporting_fx` and Desk's Portfolio → Performance
→ FX expose the same result.
It attributes completed statement-day P&L to currencies in the account's base
currency for Day, WTD, MTD and YTD. It reconciles FX plus other P&L to portfolio
value change after external flows. Partial periods expose missing dates and
omit totals; this is valuation attribution, not realised tax-lot P&L.
See https://osauer.dev/canary/docs/start/reporting.html#fx-contribution.

Use it for:

- account, position, daily P&L, exposure, technical, and order-lifecycle reads;
- the Action Queue and daemon-composed daily brief;
- the 19-rule desk rulebook, operator-authored risk policy and its plausibility
  check, and Flex-backed reconciliation;
- current option-strategy grouping, read-only protection proposals, and
  option-exercise opportunity review;
- explicit freshness, entitlement, source-health, warning-code, and session
  context; and
- Go programs reading the daemon through `github.com/osauer/canary/v2`, or
  building on the clean-room `pkg/ibkr` protocol package.

The MCP server exposes read-only tools for status, trading status, settings,
open orders, order history, one-order status, account, positions, option
strategies, named-symbol technical analysis, detailed regime and portfolio stress, brief, broker-reporting status and the
statement performance series, FX contribution, lending fee history, indicative
borrowing-rate research, market context, FINRA short-interest screens, Edge,
rules, the policy plausibility check, proposals, opportunities, portfolio
allocation, reconciliation status,
market quotes and price history, exchange sessions, and official macro calendars
and publications. It has no MCP resources, settings writes, order previews, or
execution tools. Breadth and gamma remain daemon inputs. Use
`canary_regime` for the eight-indicator market dashboard and `canary_stress` for
full portfolio-risk evidence; the daily brief remains the summary.

Standard downloads cannot place, modify, cancel, or exercise orders. A separate
opt-in `canary-trading` binary exposes constrained CLI and app order actions with
fresh confirmation/preflight, account and mode pins, journaling, daemon policy,
and the runtime freeze gate. Trading builds also support explicitly pre-authorised defensive proposals within the existing policy and execution gates.
Since v3.18, a protective stop guard in trading builds writes on its own, but
only shrinks or cancels stop orders Canary itself placed when the position falls
below them. Stops placed by hand are never changed. A freeze holds a shrink but
not a cancel, and every other write gate still applies.

Product v3 releases ship as signed binaries, installer output, MCPB, and app
assets. The public Go module deliberately remains `/v2`; its `@latest` resolves
to the maintained v2 module line and does not install the product v3 binary.
